sources.qual: fixture — hand-written test data from the design mockups, not analysis

snapshot.one_liner: Software and computing infrastructure that businesses, governments, and individuals run on.

overview.mission: To empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more.
overview.what_it_does: Microsoft builds the software and computing infrastructure that businesses, governments, and individuals run on.
overview.how_it_makes_money: Most of the money now arrives as subscriptions and consumption contracts rather than one-time license sales, so a customer keeps paying while they keep using the product.

rows.name: Microsoft 365 Commercial Products and Cloud Services

customers.who: Large enterprises and government bodies carry the business: they rent Azure capacity to run their systems and buy Microsoft 365 seats for their staff.
customers.why: Enterprises choose Azure over Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud largely on fit, since the servers, databases, and tools their teams use come from the same supplier.

predictable_revenue.note: Roughly 70% of revenue comes from cloud consumption and per-seat subscriptions that renew without a fresh buying decision, and revenue rose in each of the last seven quarters.

pricing_power.note: Operating margin edged up to 45.1% in the June quarter while revenue grew 17.7%, and a paid AI tier was added on top of subscriptions customers already had.

recession_proof.note: The two biggest lines are cloud infrastructure and workplace software that businesses must run to operate, and advertising, the first budget cut in a downturn, is only 4.6% of revenue.

competitive_position.note: Return on invested capital of 25.3% is roughly double the 12.6% median of its comparison group, and it holds a category-defining position in both segments that drive revenue.

phase.stage_note: Profitable, still growing, and returning capital through dividends and buybacks.

drivers.name: Switching costs
drivers.note: Identity, email, files and line-of-business apps are wired together; moving one piece means re-plumbing the rest.

drivers.name: Distribution
drivers.note: Hundreds of millions of existing commercial seats give every new product, like the AI tier, a built-in sales channel.

drivers.name: Scale
drivers.note: Datacenter build-out at this size spreads fixed cost across more customers than almost any rival can.

moat.note: The moat is the bundle: each product makes the others harder to leave.

drivers.name: Azure AI consumption
drivers.note: Model hosting and inference is the fastest-growing slice of cloud spend.

drivers.name: Paid AI seats
drivers.note: An add-on priced on top of existing Microsoft 365 subscriptions.

drivers.name: Security
drivers.note: Sold into the same enterprise accounts, raising revenue per customer.

growth.note: Growth now leans on AI attach to an installed base rather than on winning new logos.

management.note: Led the pivot from Windows licensing to cloud subscriptions.
management.capital_allocation_note: Heavy datacenter capex alongside a steadily rising dividend and ongoing buybacks.

risks.name: AI capex payback
risks.note: Datacenter spending is running ahead of the revenue it is meant to earn; a slower AI uptake would compress free cash flow.

risks.name: Antitrust pressure
risks.note: Bundling of Teams and cloud licensing terms are under regulator review in the EU and US.

risks.name: Cloud price competition
risks.note: Amazon and Google can cut compute prices to win AI workloads.

risks.name: Gaming weakness
risks.note: Gaming revenue fell 7% and the segment is small enough not to move the whole.

bull_points: Recurring revenue base that renews without a fresh buying decision
AI tier monetises the existing seat base at high incremental margin
ROIC roughly double the peer median
bear_points: Price / free cash flow of 56.9x leaves little room for disappointment
Free cash flow growth (+4% 3-yr) lags earnings growth because of capex
